statement: If from a straight line there be subtracted a straight line which is incommensurable in square with the whole, and which with the whole makes the sum of the squares on them medial, but twice the rectangle contained by them rational, the remainder is irrational: and let it be called that which produces with a rational area a medial whole.
heath_proof: For from the straight line AB let there be subtracted the straight line BC which is incommensurable in square with AB and fulfils the given conditions; [X. 34] I say that the remainder AC is the irrational straight line aforesaid. For, since the sum of the squares on AB, BC is medial, while twice the rectangle AB, BC is rational, therefore the squares on AB, BC are incommensurable with twice the rectangle AB, BC; therefore the remainder also, the square on AC, is incommensurable with twice the rectangle AB, BC. [II. 7, X. 16] And twice the rectangle AB, BC is rational; therefore the square on AC is irrational; therefore AC is irrational. And let it be called that which produces with a rational area a medial whole.

**Statement:** If from a straight line there be subtracted a straight line which is incommensurable in square with the whole, and which with the whole makes the sum of the squares on them medial, but twice the rectangle contained by them rational, the remainder is irrational: and let it be called that which produces with a rational area a medial whole.

**Step 1.** Let AB be a straight line, and from AB let there be subtracted the straight line BC, so that C lies on AB and AC is the remainder. Suppose that BC is incommensurable in square with the whole AB, that the sum of the squares on AB and BC is medial, and that twice the rectangle AB, BC is rational. We must show that the remainder AC is irrational.

**Step 2.** Since the straight line AB is cut at C, the squares on AB and BC taken together are equal to twice the rectangle AB, BC together with the square on AC [2.7]. Thus the sum of the squares on AB, BC is a whole composed of exactly two parts, namely twice the rectangle AB, BC and the square on AC.

**Step 3.** Let a rational straight line be set out; its square is the rational area with reference to which areas are called rational or irrational [D10.1.4]. The sum of the squares on AB, BC is medial, that is, it is equal to the square on a medial straight line, which is a rectangle contained by rational straight lines commensurable in square only; such an area is irrational [10.21], i.e. incommensurable with the rational square [D10.1.4]. On the other hand, twice the rectangle AB, BC is rational, so it is commensurable with the rational square [D10.1.4].

**Step 4.** Twice the rectangle AB, BC is commensurable with the rational square, while the rational square is incommensurable with the sum of the squares on AB, BC [Step 3]; therefore twice the rectangle AB, BC is incommensurable with the sum of the squares on AB, BC [10.13].

**Step 5.** The whole, namely the sum of the squares on AB, BC, is therefore incommensurable with one of its two parts, twice the rectangle AB, BC [Step 2, Step 4]. Hence the two parts are incommensurable with one another: the square on AC is incommensurable with twice the rectangle AB, BC [10.16].

**Step 6.** Twice the rectangle AB, BC is commensurable with the rational square [Step 3], and it is incommensurable with the square on AC [Step 5]; therefore the square on AC is incommensurable with the rational square [10.13]. Hence the square on AC is an irrational area [D10.1.4].

**Step 7.** The square on AC is irrational, and AC is the side of that square; therefore the straight line AC is irrational [D10.1.4]. And let AC be called that which produces with a rational area a medial whole, since the square on AC added to the rational area twice the rectangle AB, BC makes up the medial whole, the sum of the squares on AB, BC [Step 2]. Q.E.D.
